title: Finite Field
body:
A [[Field]] with finitely many elements. Also called a **Galois field** and written $GF(q)$ or
$\mathbb{F}_q$; both names are in use and the applications almost always write $GF$.

This is where the course lands, and it is the note two other subjects in the vault need.

## The classification

**A finite field exists if and only if its size is a prime power, and for each $p^n$ there is
exactly one up to [[Isomorphism]].**

$$|F| = p^n, \qquad p \text{ prime}, \; n \ge 1$$

Both halves have short reasons:

- **Why a prime power.** $\operatorname{char}(F)$ is a prime $p$ (see [[Field]]), so $F$ contains
  a copy of $\mathbb{Z}_p$, and $F$ is a [[Vector Space]] over it. A finite-dimensional vector
  space of dimension $n$ over a $p$-element field has $p^n$ elements, because an element is a
  tuple of $n$ coordinates. So the count is forced by [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]], not by field theory.
- **Why exactly one.** Any two fields of the same size are isomorphic. There is no choice being
  made, which is why "the" field of order 256 is a legitimate phrase even though the polynomial
  you build it with is a choice.

## Building them

| $n$ | Construction |
|---|---|
| $n = 1$ | $GF(p) = \mathbb{Z}_p$, plain [[Modular Arithmetic]] |
| $n > 1$ | $GF(p^n) = \mathbb{Z}_p[x]/(f)$ for any irreducible $f$ of degree $n$ |

**$\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}$ is not it.** $\mathbb{Z}_4$ is not a field: 2 is a zero divisor. The
prime-power fields are quotients of a [[Polynomial Ring]], not of $\mathbb{Z}$, and that
distinction is the most common mistake in the block. See [[Field Extension]] and
[[Irreducibility]].

One more structural fact, small but load-bearing: **the non-zero elements of a finite field form
a [[Cyclic Group]]** under multiplication, of order $q - 1$. So there is a single generator whose
powers run through every non-zero element, which is what makes log tables (and fast
implementations) possible.

## $GF(2)$ is the one you already use

$GF(2) = \{0, 1\}$ with addition mod 2 and multiplication mod 2:

```
+ | 0 1        × | 0 1
--+----        --+----
0 | 0 1        0 | 0 0
1 | 1 0        1 | 0 1

addition is XOR,  multiplication is AND
```

In characteristic 2 every element is its own additive inverse, so **subtraction and addition are
the same operation**. That is why parity, checksums, and linear codes are all XOR and nothing
else. [[Boolean Algebra]] in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] is describing this field's operations from
the circuit side, and a parity bit is a linear equation over $GF(2)$: see [[Error Detection]].

## $GF(2^8)$, the field a byte lives in

Represent a [[Byte]] as a polynomial of degree $< 8$ over $GF(2)$, one bit per coefficient.
Addition is bitwise XOR. Multiplication is polynomial multiplication reduced modulo a fixed
irreducible degree-8 polynomial, so the product is a byte again.

```
0x53 = 01010011 = x⁶ + x⁴ + x + 1
AES reduces modulo x⁸ + x⁴ + x³ + x + 1

byte + byte  =  XOR
byte × byte  =  carry-less multiply, then reduce
```

Two consequences that make it worth the trouble:

- **Every non-zero byte has an inverse.** That is what $\mathbb{Z}_{256}$ cannot give you, and it
  is exactly what a cipher needs for an invertible non-linear step. The AES S-box *is* inversion
  in $GF(2^8)$, which is why [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111) lists this course as its prerequisite.
- **Bytes can be treated as scalars in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]].** Matrices over $GF(2^8)$ are
  invertible under the usual conditions, which is what AES's MixColumn step and Reed-Solomon
  coding both rely on.

## The error-handling ladder

This note is the algebra rung of a three-rung story the vault tells across three folders:

| Course | Owns |
|---|---|
| [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) | **detection.** [[Error Detection]] covers parity checking on the 68000: a single-bit error is noticed, not repaired |
| [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] (`Books/`) | **correction.** [[Error Correcting Code]]: Hamming and Reed-Solomon, recovering the byte rather than just flagging it |
| MATH 2101 | **the algebra.** Why arithmetic on bytes is a field at all, and where the codewords come from |

Reed-Solomon treats a block of bytes as coefficients of a polynomial over $GF(2^8)$ and sends its
values at fixed points. Any $k$ of those values determine a degree-$(k-1)$ polynomial uniquely, by
the same at-most-$n$-roots argument in [[Polynomial Ring]], so extra values are pure redundancy
and a lost or corrupted symbol can be reconstructed. That is what a CD, a QR code, and a RAID
array are each doing.
